title: Manufacture of a functional human oocyte from a somatic cell

concept.text: The innovation would turn the nuclear genome of an ordinary body cell, such as a skin cell, into the genetic contribution of a developmentally competent human egg. The resulting oocyte would need to undergo accurate chromosome reduction and recombination, establish appropriate maternal genomic imprints, and contain the cellular machinery needed for fertilization and early embryonic development. Function would therefore mean more than an egg-like appearance or the ability to divide after sperm injection.

Two levels of manufacture need to be distinguished. One could supply a somatic-cell-derived nuclear genome while relying on an enucleated donor egg for cytoplasm, maternal factors and mitochondria. A more complete achievement would manufacture the competent oocyte without consuming a donor egg. The former could establish a new source of nuclear genetic parenthood, but would retain donor-egg dependence and would not make every component of the oocyte originate from the somatic-cell donor.

significance.text: The revolutionary consequence would be a new route to genetic parenthood for some people who lack usable oocytes. IVF enables fertilization in the laboratory but still requires a competent egg; successful somatic-cell conversion would address the availability of that essential gamete. This could matter after gonadal failure, some cancer treatments, loss of ovaries or reproductive aging. Eligibility would remain individual: these conditions do not invariably eliminate usable oocytes, and previously preserved eggs or embryos can already preserve reproductive options.

A reliable laboratory supply could also expand research and, conditionally, treatment. However, the supply benefit depends on production efficiency and the source of the egg's cytoplasm. Replacing a donor egg's nucleus with a somatic genome changes whose nuclear genes the egg carries; it does not by itself increase the net supply of donor-independent eggs. Removing that bottleneck would require competent oocyte production without consuming existing donor oocytes.

Impact synthesis: comparison with IVF describes the scale of a possible enabling advance, not evidence of equivalent readiness or universal access. Producing an oocyte would not automatically correct inherited variants, acquired mutations or other defects in its source genome. It would also leave gestation without a functioning uterus and safe clinical embryo editing as separate capabilities. Benefits would depend on which source cells and patients can be served safely, how reproducibly eggs can be produced, and whether reproductive use becomes ethically and legally permissible.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unresolved capability in the supplied human studies is coordinated production of a mature, developmentally competent oocyte from a somatic nuclear genome. Normal human oocyte development begins in fetal life and extends to reproductive maturity over more than a decade. Its timing and biology differ from those of mice, so the successful mouse pathway cannot simply be assumed to transfer to humans. Human germ-cell expansion is an intermediate achievement; it does not establish successful meiotic entry, maturation or reproductive competence.

Chromosome reduction must preserve a balanced genetic complement while reproducing the required meiotic processes. Canonical meiosis coordinates homologous chromosome pairing, crossover recombination and segregation. An experimentally induced division that distributes chromosomes randomly without crossovers can reduce chromosome number, but does not reproduce that mechanism. The 2025 human experiment illustrates the distinction: numerical reduction and blastocyst formation occurred, yet all analyzed embryos had chromosome imbalances.

Epigenetic and cytoplasmic competence are additional barriers. Erasing inappropriate somatic or inherited imprint information is distinct from subsequently establishing the maternal imprints required in an egg. The cell must also acquire maternal factors and competent mitochondria that support development after fertilization. Donor-oocyte cytoplasm supplies such components in the experimental nuclear-transfer route, leaving open how to generate them reliably without donor eggs.

current_state.text: In 2016, Hikabe and colleagues reported reconstitution of mouse oogenesis from pluripotent stem cells, including induced pluripotent stem cells derived from adult tail fibroblasts. They generated mature oocytes and obtained offspring, providing a functional animal demonstration rather than merely germ-cell markers or early embryos. The supplied review assessed a subscription preview containing the abstract, editorial summary and figure legends, rather than the complete main paper. Those materials support the broad reported achievement; detailed outcomes and the figures were not independently assessed, and the separately supplied PDF was supplementary information.

Murase, Saitou and colleagues, in work published online on 20 May 2024 in Nature 631:170–178, reported human germ-cell-like-cell differentiation into mitotic pro-spermatogonia or oogonia-like cells. Expansion reached approximately ten-billion-fold or more in some cell lines, with substantial variation between lines. This was not production of mature human oocytes: the reported cells did not upregulate meiosis genes, and meiotic entry remained deficient. The retained XML extraction was truncated during extended-data material, although the relevant abstract, results and discussion were available to the supplied review.

On 30 September 2025, Marti Gutierrez, Mitalipov and colleagues reported transferring human skin-cell genomes into enucleated donor oocytes and inducing a reductive division termed mitomeiosis. Homologous chromosome segregation was random and lacked crossover recombination. All analyzed embryos exhibited chromosome imbalances. The experiment therefore demonstrated an experimental route to chromosome reduction and early development, without establishing normally functioning human gametes.

For 82 sperm-injected somatic-cell nuclear-transfer oocytes receiving assisted activation, the 2025 paper reported mean blastocyst development of 8.8% ± 5.2% across experiments. This is an experimental summary of blastocyst formation, not a rate of normal embryos or successful reproduction. OHSU's accompanying report rounded the result to about 9%. Development was studied only through the blastocyst stage, with research ending by day 6; no pregnancy was attempted. The route consumed donor oocytes and remained a proof of concept.

The institutional report's description of functional eggs should be interpreted within these experimental limits. Its headline and idealized description of diploid embryos do not override the primary paper's finding of chromosome imbalances in every analyzed embryo. The supplied review had complete primary-paper text for the 2025 result, but did not independently inspect the figures or underlying sequencing datasets. That limitation bounds independent verification; it is not evidence that the reported experiment was false.

Evidence boundary: the supplied studies document a progression from functional mouse oogenesis to human germ-cell intermediates and experimental human chromosome reduction. They do not demonstrate the target human reproductive capability. The supplied freshness record contains no assessment of subsequent work, so these results do not establish whether the gap remained open on 1 November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: reproducibly derive human oocytes whose nuclear genomes originate from adult somatic cells, without using a donor-oocyte nucleus as the nuclear genetic source. Directly demonstrate accurate meiotic chromosome reduction and recombination, appropriate maternal imprint establishment and cytoplasmic competence. Fertilization should produce euploid embryos with appropriate parental imprints. A chromosomally abnormal blastocyst would not meet this proposal, and euploidy alone would not establish all the other required properties.
completion_criteria.label: Functional somatic-derived human oocytes produce appropriately imprinted euploid embryos

completion_criteria.text: Proposed preclinical and human endpoints: species-matched large-animal experiments yielding healthy offspring with longitudinal follow-up would provide valuable preclinical validation of an analogous process. They could not substitute for demonstrating human reproductive competence, and the supplied evidence establishes no system in which human embryos could complete reproductive development in another species. If ethical and regulatory conditions permit human reproductive testing, healthy births followed by longitudinal assessment of development would provide further evidence of the human capability.
completion_criteria.label: Healthy human births with longitudinal assessment of development

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements: prespecify meaningful efficiency and quality benchmarks, report failures and chromosome abnormalities, and reproduce results across independent experiments, laboratories and multiple somatic-cell donors. Evaluate variation across relevant donor ages and source-cell conditions, including the integrity of the source genome. The supplied evidence does not establish numerical acceptance thresholds; these would need justification before testing. Finite studies would establish the breadth actually demonstrated, rather than safety or applicability for every person.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible results across laboratories and donors against prespecified benchmarks

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: report donor-oocyte consumption, mitochondrial origin and dependence on donor cytoplasmic factors explicitly. A successful donor-cytoplasm route could satisfy the narrower demonstration of somatic nuclear-genome conversion. Whole-oocyte manufacture would additionally require production without consuming donor eggs. Efficiency must be sufficient for reliable use at the claimed scope, rather than an isolated successful embryo or birth.
completion_criteria.label: Report donor-oocyte dependence and efficiency sufficient for claimed use

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: OBG-05, Reversal of human ovarian reproductive aging, is the closest related concept. OBG-02 would generate an oocyte from a somatic nuclear genome; OBG-05 would reverse reproductive aging in the ovary. Their overlap includes oocyte quality, reproductive aging mechanisms, infertility treatment and the need to validate reproductive outcomes. This is broader than a shared concern with age-related infertility, but does not make the interventions interchangeable.

Roster-based synthesis: OBG-08, A manufactured uterus that supports pregnancy without a donor graft and chronic immunosuppression, concerns the organ supporting gestation. OBG-03, Extrauterine physiological support across the viability gap, concerns support at a later developmental stage. Either could eventually complement an oocyte-derived route to reproduction, but neither supplies competent gametes, and producing an oocyte does not establish either gestational capability.

Roster-based synthesis: OBG-06, In utero molecular correction of fetal-onset genetic disease, addresses disease after conception. It remains distinct from producing an egg: a somatic-cell-derived oocyte would not inherently correct variants carried by its source genome. OBG-09, Fertility-preserving interception of high-grade serous tubo-ovarian carcinoma, seeks to intercept cancer while preserving fertility; manufacturing oocytes would instead offer a possible new gamete source and would not itself prevent or treat cancer.

Roster-based synthesis: OBG-01, Causal control of the human parturition clock; OBG-04, In utero reversal of placental insufficiency; and OBG-10, Restoration of the amniotic compartment after preterm membrane rupture, address timing or physiological support during an established pregnancy. OBG-07, A mechanism-based cure for endometriosis, addresses a disease that can affect reproductive health. These concepts share possible reproductive outcomes with OBG-02 while targeting different mechanisms. The supplied roster provides titles rather than full specifications, so these comparisons describe broad distinctions without assigning detailed mechanisms or completion requirements to those entries.

change_log.change: Clarified the distinction between somatic nuclear-genome conversion using donor cytoplasm and manufacture of an entire oocyte without donor eggs.
change_log.reason: The candidate's original completion criterion permits donor cytoplasm, while its supply implications could be read as eliminating donor-egg dependence.

change_log.change: Separated epigenetic erasure from maternal imprint establishment and added cytoplasmic competence to the target capability.
change_log.reason: Imprint resetting alone does not describe the required maternal epigenetic state, and a suitable nuclear genome alone cannot support early development.

change_log.change: Explained why random chromosome reduction without crossover recombination differs from canonical meiosis.
change_log.reason: The 2025 experiment demonstrated numerical reduction but did not establish the coordinated meiotic mechanism required by the concept.

change_log.change: Qualified the genetic-parenthood claim to account for residual function and previously preserved reproductive material.
change_log.reason: Age, gonadal failure, cancer treatment or absence of ovaries does not invariably eliminate all existing routes to genetic parenthood.

change_log.change: Preserved the 2024 expansion magnitude while adding line-dependent variation and the absence of demonstrated mature oocytes.
change_log.reason: Large expansion of mitotic germ-cell intermediates should not be mistaken for successful human oogenesis.

change_log.change: Replaced the approximate 2025 blastocyst description with the reported 8.8% ± 5.2% experimental mean, its 82-oocyte denominator and assisted-activation context.
change_log.reason: The precise reporting distinguishes blastocyst development from normal-embryo production and successful reproduction.

change_log.change: Specified that all analyzed 2025 embryos had chromosome imbalances and retained the day-6 limit, donor-oocyte dependence and absence of pregnancy attempts.
change_log.reason: The primary paper provides a more informative boundary than the original wording about widespread abnormalities or the institutional headline.

change_log.change: Separated species-matched large-animal validation from demonstration of human reproductive competence.
change_log.reason: Animal offspring cannot serve as an alternative completion endpoint for the human capability.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed completion criteria to include direct meiotic verification, independent replication, defined practical scope and explicit donor-cytoplasm accounting.
change_log.reason: These requirements make the intended demonstration assessable without inventing consensus thresholds or claiming literal universality.

change_log.change: Preserved source-access limitations and confined the state-of-field assessment to the supplied dated evidence.
change_log.reason: The 2016 source was a subscription preview, the 2024 extraction was partial, underlying 2025 datasets were not independently assessed, and no later-work freshness assessment was supplied.

change_log.change: Broadened the OBG-05 comparison and explained distinctions with every other supplied roster entry.
change_log.reason: Ovarian rejuvenation overlaps in more than age-related infertility, while the remaining concepts address separate reproductive or gestational capabilities.

unresolved_issues: The supplied freshness record does not establish whether later work changed the field's position between the September 2025 study and 1 November 2026.

The concept's ultimate scope remains ambiguous between somatic nuclear-genome conversion using donor cytoplasm and whole-oocyte manufacture without donor eggs; both scopes are distinguished rather than silently choosing one.
No numerical efficiency, abnormality-rate or follow-up-duration thresholds are established by the supplied evidence. Suitable proposed benchmarks require further justification.
The supplied evidence does not establish which human source-cell types, donor ages or genome conditions could support safe and reproducible reproductive use.

Detailed independent assessment remains limited by the 2016 subscription preview, the truncated 2024 extraction and the absence of independent inspection of the 2025 figures and underlying sequencing datasets.
Only titles were supplied for the other roster entries. Their precise technical scope and detailed overlaps cannot be verified from those titles alone.

brief.title: Human eggs made from ordinary body cells
possible: People who lack usable eggs could have a new route to genetically related children. An ordinary body cell, such as a skin cell, could supply the genetic material for an egg capable of supporting fertilization and development.
why: This could expand reproductive options after loss of ovaries, some cancer treatments or reproductive aging. Producing eggs without consuming donated eggs could also expand the supply for research and fertility treatment.

sources.who: Orie Hikabe, Katsuhiko Hayashi and colleagues
sources.showed: They made mature mouse eggs from stem cells, including cells reprogrammed from adult tail tissue, and obtained offspring.
sources.quote: Fully potent mature oocytes were generated in culture from embryonic stem cells and from induced pluripotent stem cells derived from both embryonic fibroblasts and adult tail tip fibroblasts.
sources.cited_for: Mouse experiments demonstrate that body-cell-derived eggs can support reproduction.
sources.not_established: Human egg development differs from mouse development, and human reproductive competence remains unproven.

sources.who: Yusuke Murase, Mitinori Saitou and colleagues
sources.showed: They grew large quantities of human reproductive precursor cells, including cells resembling early egg precursors.
sources.quote: These cells fail to fully activate genes vital for spermatogenesis and oogenesis, and their promoters remain methylated.
sources.cited_for: Human reproductive precursors can be expanded, while cells missing a DNA-resetting enzyme fail to activate key reproductive genes.
sources.not_established: The cells had yet to enter the specialized chromosome division needed to become mature eggs.

sources.who: Nuria Marti Gutierrez, Shoukhrat Mitalipov and colleagues
sources.showed: They placed human skin-cell genetic material into donor eggs whose own genetic material had been removed. Assisted division and fertilization produced early embryos.
sources.quote: Comprehensive chromosome tracing via sequencing revealed that homologous chromosome segregation occurred randomly and without crossover recombination.
sources.cited_for: Human skin-cell genetic material can undergo experimental chromosome reduction and contribute to early embryos.
sources.not_established: Every analyzed embryo had chromosome imbalances, and the process consumed donor eggs.

sources.showed: Their institutional report described the same skin-cell experiment. About 9% reached the blastocyst stage, an early embryo stage.
sources.quote: Researchers at Oregon Health & Science University have accomplished a unique proof of concept to treat infertility by turning skin cells into eggs capable of producing early human embryos.
sources.cited_for: The report describes how far embryos developed in the human experiment.
sources.not_established: No pregnancy was attempted, and early embryo development did not establish reproductive safety.

shown: Hikabe and colleagues obtained mouse offspring from laboratory-made eggs. In humans, Murase and colleagues grew egg precursors, while Marti Gutierrez and colleagues used donated eggs to produce early embryos carrying skin-cell and sperm genetic material.
missing: Human eggs still need accurate chromosome halving and recombination, the exchange of DNA between matching chromosomes.
They must establish maternal imprints, chemical marks that control gene activity according to parental origin.
They must acquire the cellular machinery and energy supply needed to support development after fertilization.
Complete egg manufacture still requires a way to supply these components without consuming donor eggs.

milestones.label: Human eggs produce embryos with balanced chromosomes and imprints
milestones.explanation: Body-cell-derived eggs would need accurate chromosome division, DNA exchange, maternal marks and cellular machinery, yielding embryos with balanced chromosomes and parental marks. This would establish coordinated egg function.

milestones.label: Healthy human births with long-term developmental follow-up
milestones.explanation: Large-animal offspring would provide preclinical support, followed by healthy human births and developmental follow-up if reproductive testing is permitted. Human outcomes would establish reproductive competence.

milestones.label: Independent laboratories reproduce results across donors
milestones.explanation: Independent laboratories would need to meet predetermined quality and efficiency benchmarks across donors and source-cell conditions, reporting failures. This would establish how reliably the process works and whom it can serve.

milestones.label: Donor-egg dependence and efficiency match the claimed use
milestones.explanation: Results would need to identify donor-egg consumption, the origin of cellular energy structures and reliance on donor cell contents, with adequate efficiency. Complete egg manufacture would require production without consuming donor eggs.

uncertain: Which body-cell types, donor ages and genetic conditions can support safe, reproducible reproduction remains open.
Suitable thresholds for efficiency, chromosome abnormalities and developmental follow-up still need justification.
The eventual capability could depend on donated egg contents or extend to making the entire egg without them.

page.title: Human oocyte in vitro gametogenesis from somatic cells
page.definition: The goal is to grow a human oocyte (egg cell) in the laboratory from a reprogrammed somatic cell, such as a blood or skin cell. The egg would carry the somatic-cell donor’s genome and could support development to live birth after fertilization. The egg itself develops from the reprogrammed cell, without using cytoplasm from a donated egg. This form of in vitro gametogenesis has produced offspring in mice.

goal.need: Estimates of premature ovarian insufficiency unrelated to medical treatment range from about 1% to 3.5% of women. For those who have no usable eggs, donor eggs offer a route to pregnancy, but the egg’s genome comes from the donor. IVF needs an existing egg. If safety for patients and children can be established, an egg grown from a patient’s own cells could allow them to have a genetically related child. Laboratory-grown eggs could also reduce the need for egg donation for early-embryo research.

statements.quote: addressing infertility because of absence of or inability to produce mature gametes
statements.context: One of the committee's proposed applications of in vitro gametogenesis.

statements.body: International Society for Stem Cell Research, Guidelines Task Force
statements.quote: reducing the need for gamete donors
statements.context: The passage lists reasons to derive human gametes, including supplying oocytes for early-embryo research.

statements.quote: Conception’s mission is to turn stem cells into human eggs and redefine fertility.

statements.body: International Society for Stem Cell Research
statements.quote: If the safety, policy, and regulatory issues are resolved, this approach may be desirable
statements.context: Section 2.2.3A(c) of the Guidelines for Stem Cell Research and Clinical Translation places fertilization for human reproduction using stem-cell-derived gametes in Category 3A, currently not permitted. It identifies infertility after childhood cancer treatment as a possible future indication.

completion.title: A human oocyte made from a somatic cell without a donor egg produces a live birth.
completion.criterion: At least one live birth follows fertilization of a human oocyte produced from a traceable somatic-cell-derived line without donor-oocyte cytoplasm. Genetic testing establishes nuclear contributions from the somatic-cell donor and the sperm donor. Apply ICMART's live-birth definition: delivery after 22 completed gestational weeks with breathing or another sign of life; a birth weight of at least 500 g can substitute when gestational age is unknown.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no adopted IVG-specific completion criterion was located.
completion.basis: The 2025 ICMART glossary, published in 2026, defines live birth. The Atlas uses one such birth with verified egg origin and nuclear parentage as a demonstration of reproductive competence. No adopted IVG-specific completion rule was identified. A single birth cannot establish the frequency of adverse outcomes or long-term safety.

milestones.title: Somatic-cell-derived mammalian oocytes yield live offspring after fertilization.
milestones.criterion: Oocytes derived from reprogrammed mammalian somatic cells without donor-oocyte cytoplasm give rise after fertilization to zygotes, embryos and live offspring of the same species.
milestones.set_by: Field convention for functional gamete validation described by the ISSCR Guidelines Task Force in its 2021 update.
milestones.threshold_quote: capable of giving rise to zygotes after fertilization and then to embryos and live born animals.

milestones.title: Human somatic-cell-derived germ cells enter meiosis and become primary oocytes.
milestones.criterion: Human germ cells derived from reprogrammed somatic cells enter the first meiotic division and acquire primary-oocyte identity.
milestones.set_by: Biological stage convention described in HFEA SCAAC paper HFEA (07/10/2026) 010, section 1.1; this is a cell-identity criterion, not treatment authorisation.
milestones.threshold_quote: enter meiosis during foetal development to form primary oocytes.

milestones.title: Human IVG oocytes have the correct chromosomes, meiotic recombination and maternal imprints.
milestones.criterion: Human oocytes produced from somatic cells without donor-oocyte cytoplasm have the correct chromosome complement, evidence of meiotic recombination and molecular markers of maturation. Germline epigenetic remodelling is recapitulated and maternal genomic imprints, parent-specific gene-regulatory marks, are established normally. The setting document supplies qualitative requirements without numerical acceptance limits.
milestones.set_by: UK Regulatory Horizons Council, 10 July 2026 advisory report, sections 2.4.1–2.4.2; proposed preclinical evidence requirements, not licensing criteria.
milestones.threshold_quote: correct chromosome number, evidence of meiotic recombination

milestones.title: Human IVG embryos behave like conventional IVF embryos in comparative developmental tests.
milestones.criterion: Embryos formed with human oocytes grown from somatic cells without donor-oocyte cytoplasm are compared with embryos formed by conventional IVF. The comparison shows comparable morphology, progression through developmental milestones and molecular signatures at corresponding stages. The Council specifies no numerical equivalence margin.
milestones.set_by: UK Regulatory Horizons Council, 10 July 2026 advisory report, section 2.4.3; proposed comparative embryo evidence requirement.
milestones.threshold_quote: Evidence that embryos created using IVG behave like embryos created using conventional IVF

milestones.title: Nonhuman-primate IVG oocytes yield offspring with reproducible evidence of safety across generations.
milestones.criterion: Species-matched nonhuman-primate IVG produces oocytes that support fertilization, embryo development and offspring whose health across generations provides reliable, reproducible safety evidence. ASRM makes this a prerequisite to human trials. It specifies no minimum animal count, number of generations, abnormality-rate cutoff or follow-up duration.
milestones.set_by: American Society for Reproductive Medicine, 2026 Ethics Committee opinion, 'Preclinical pathway and biological safety requirements for IVG'; qualitative prerequisite.
milestones.threshold_quote: reliable, reproducible safety data in primates

milestones.title: A pregnancy from a human somatic-cell-derived oocyte shows fetal cardiac activity.
milestones.criterion: After transfer of an embryo formed with a human somatic-cell-derived oocyte made without donor-oocyte cytoplasm, ultrasonography or clinical examination documents at least one fetus with discernible cardiac activity.
milestones.set_by: ICMART and collaborating societies, The International Glossary on Infertility and Fertility Care, 2025, clinical pregnancy with fetal cardiac activity.
milestones.threshold_quote: at least one fetus with discernible cardiac activity.

milestones.title: Reprogrammed human somatic cells give rise to primordial germ cell-like cells.
milestones.criterion: Human induced pluripotent stem cells derived from somatic cells differentiate into primordial germ cell-like cells, the laboratory counterparts of the early precursors shared by eggs and sperm.
milestones.set_by: Human germ-cell stage convention described by the HFEA Scientific and Clinical Advances Advisory Committee, October 2026, section 2.3.
milestones.threshold_quote: hPGCLCs can be generated from diverse somatic cell sources

milestones.title: Reprogrammed human somatic cells give rise to oogonia-like cells.
milestones.criterion: Human germ cells derived from reprogrammed somatic cells acquire the identity of oogonia, the proliferating female germ cells that precede primary oocytes.
milestones.set_by: Human germ-cell stage convention described by the HFEA Scientific and Clinical Advances Advisory Committee, October 2026, sections 1.1 and 2.5.
milestones.threshold_quote: generation of oogonia-like cells from iPSCs

milestones.title: A human somatic-cell-derived oocyte reaches metaphase II in vitro.
milestones.criterion: An oocyte grown from reprogrammed human somatic cells without donor-oocyte cytoplasm resumes meiosis, completes its first meiotic division and reaches metaphase of the second division in culture.
milestones.set_by: ICMART and collaborating societies, The International Glossary on Infertility and Fertility Care, 2025, definitions of nuclear maturation and oocyte maturation.
milestones.threshold_quote: resumes meiosis and progresses from prophase I to metaphase II.

milestones.title: A fertilized human somatic-cell-derived oocyte forms a zygote with two pronuclei.
milestones.criterion: After insemination of a human somatic-cell-derived oocyte made without donor-oocyte cytoplasm, two pronuclei are observed in the zygote. For static assessment after conventional IVF or intracytoplasmic sperm injection, the consensus observation window is 16–17 hours after insemination.
milestones.set_by: ESHRE and Alpha Scientists in Reproductive Medicine, 2025 Istanbul consensus update, zygote assessment. Its morphological fertilization criterion is applied here to an IVG oocyte.
milestones.threshold_quote: A designation of normal fertilization typically relies on observation of two PN.

milestones.title: Human IVG oocytes show the correct chromosome number, meiotic recombination and maturation markers.
milestones.criterion: Human oocytes grown from somatic cells without donor-oocyte cytoplasm have the chromosome complement appropriate to their stage, show evidence of meiotic recombination and express molecular markers appropriate to maturation. The Council specifies no numerical acceptance rate.
milestones.set_by: UK Regulatory Horizons Council, 2026 advisory report, section 2.4.1, proposed preclinical evidence.
milestones.threshold_quote: correct chromosome number, evidence of meiotic recombination, and appropriate molecular markers of maturation.

milestones.title: Human somatic-cell-derived oocytes acquire normal maternal genomic imprints.
milestones.criterion: Systematic epigenetic assessment of human oocytes grown from somatic cells without donor-oocyte cytoplasm shows germline epigenetic remodelling and establishment of the normal maternal imprints, the marks that regulate genes according to their parent of origin. The Council specifies no numerical acceptance rate.
milestones.set_by: UK Regulatory Horizons Council, 2026 advisory report, sections 2.3.3 and 2.4.2, proposed preclinical evidence.
milestones.threshold_quote: genomic imprints are established as normal.

not_found: No adopted human-IVG numerical limits for efficiency, chromosome abnormalities, imprinting errors or offspring follow-up were located.
No registered reproductive trial of somatic-cell-derived human oocytes was located in the ClinicalTrials.gov search.
No published donor-oocyte-independent human pregnancy or live birth, or nonhuman-primate IVG-oocyte birth, was located.

case_label = "Starting karyotype". Reason: The mouse studies distinguish the donor cell’s original sex chromosomes from those of the line that ultimately produced the egg.

definition = "The goal is to grow a human oocyte (egg cell) in the laboratory from a reprogrammed somatic cell, such as a blood or skin cell. The egg would carry the somatic-cell donor\u2019s genome and could support development to live birth after fertilization. The egg itself develops from the reprogrammed cell, without using cytoplasm from a donated egg. This form of in vitro gametogenesis has produced offspring in mice.". Reason: The present tense makes a human live birth sound demonstrated, and the definition leaves the role of donor cytoplasm unclear.

goal.need = "Estimates of premature ovarian insufficiency unrelated to medical treatment range from about 1% to 3.5% of women. For those who have no usable eggs, donor eggs offer a route to pregnancy, but the egg\u2019s genome comes from the donor. IVF needs an existing egg. If safety for patients and children can be established, an egg grown from a patient\u2019s own cells could allow them to have a genetically related child. Laboratory-grown eggs could also reduce the need for egg donation for early-embryo research.". Reason: The all-cause infertility estimate does not measure the population lacking usable eggs, and the existing rationale omits what egg donation and conventional IVF can offer them.

add statement by International Society for Stem Cell Research, 2025: "If the safety, policy, and regulatory issues are resolved, this approach may be desirable". Reason: The existing ISSCR statement covers embryo research but omits the society’s explicit position on reproductive use.

The Atlas uses one such birth with verified egg origin and nuclear parentage as a demonstration of reproductive competence. No adopted IVG-specific completion rule was identified. A single birth cannot establish the frequency of adverse outcomes or long-term safety."; refs = [17, 6, 2, 3, 5]. add milestone after None: "Reprogrammed human somatic cells give rise to primordial germ cell-like cells.". Reason: The entry skips the first demonstrated human germ-cell stage between a reprogrammed body cell and an oocyte precursor.

edit m1: criterion = "Oocytes derived from reprogrammed mammalian somatic cells without donor-oocyte cytoplasm give rise after fertilization to zygotes, embryos and live offspring of the same species."; set_by = "Field convention for functional gamete validation described by the ISSCR Guidelines Task Force in its 2021 update."; refs = [3, 8, 12]. Reason: The date, number of pups illustrated and description of a figure are results embedded in the mammalian live-offspring test.

add milestone after m1: "Reprogrammed human somatic cells give rise to oogonia-like cells.". Reason: Oogonia-like cells mark female germ-cell differentiation before meiosis, so their production can be judged independently of primary-oocyte formation.

edit m2: criterion = "Human germ cells derived from reprogrammed somatic cells enter the first meiotic division and acquire primary-oocyte identity."; refs = [5, 9, 4, 14]. Reason: The primary-oocyte criterion mixes the biological test with replication counts and a company claim, and omits a published human primary-oocyte study.

add milestone after m2: "A human somatic-cell-derived oocyte reaches metaphase II in vitro.". Reason: The entry jumps from meiotic entry to egg-quality tests without a distinct endpoint for nuclear maturation.

add milestone after m3: "A fertilized human somatic-cell-derived oocyte forms a zygote with two pronuclei.". Reason: Observed fertilization is a distinct human functional result that can precede a comparison of developing embryos.

split m3 into "Human IVG oocytes show the correct chromosome number, meiotic recombination and maturation markers." | "Human somatic-cell-derived oocytes acquire normal maternal genomic imprints.". Reason: Chromosome segregation and recombination can be assessed independently of maternal imprint establishment, and the Council treats them as distinct evidence requirements.

The Council specifies no numerical equivalence margin."; refs = [6]. Reason: The nuclear-transfer experiment used donated egg cytoplasm, and its blastocyst rate is an experimental result rather than an embryo-comparison threshold.
